title: Acts
intro: 40 days through the book of Acts, from Jerusalem to Rome, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Acts opens by stressing that the risen Jesus was seen, again and again: he showed himself alive with "many convincing proofs" over forty days and kept teaching about the kingdom of God. Those witnesses carry the rest of the story. Acts is the sequel to Luke's Gospel, by the same author and addressed to the same Theophilus; tradition names Luke, a doctor who traveled with Paul. Starting today, 40 days through Acts, one verse at a time.

Jesus' last words before he is taken up, and the plan for the whole book: the Holy Spirit will give his followers power to be his witnesses, starting at home and reaching the whole world. Many Christians read it as the church's mission statement. The story moves outward in widening circles: Jerusalem (chapters 1 to 7), Judea and Samaria (8 to 12), then across the Roman world to Rome. Samaria was home to a people many Jews of the time avoided.

The Ascension. On the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem, Jesus is taken up into a cloud, and two men in white speak to the stunned disciples. Their message is a promise and a nudge: Jesus will come back the same way he left, so there is no point standing and staring at the sky. Christians see here the promise of Jesus' return. Many churches mark Ascension Day forty days after Easter.

Pentecost. The Holy Spirit that Jesus promised arrives, and the disciples begin speaking in languages they never learned, so pilgrims from many nations each hear the message in their own tongue. Many Christians call this the birthday of the church, and some see it as the tower of Babel in reverse. The day was the Jewish harvest festival of Shavuot, fifty days after Passover; Pentecost is Greek for "fiftieth." Christians celebrate it fifty days after Easter.

Peter's first sermon ends with about three thousand people baptized, and Luke sums up the new community in four habits: learning from the apostles, sharing life together, breaking bread and praying. Many Christians still look to this verse as a picture of what church is meant to be. "Fellowship" is the Greek koinonia, meaning sharing or partnership. Many readers see "the breaking of bread" as shared meals that included the Lord's Supper, or communion.

Peter and John are heading into the temple for afternoon prayer when a man unable to walk since birth, carried to the gate every day to beg, asks them for money. Peter has none, but offers something better: healing. Acting "in the name of" Jesus means acting by his authority, and Acts presents the power as Jesus' own, not the apostles'. The man jumps up and goes into the temple, walking, leaping and praising God.

After the healing, Peter and John are arrested and questioned by the Sanhedrin, Jerusalem's ruling council of priests and elders. The council is astonished: these fishermen from Galilee speak with confidence, yet have no formal training in the law. It also takes note that they "had been with Jesus," and Christians take that as the point: their courage came from knowing him, not from schooling. "Unschooled" translates a Greek word meaning "unlettered."

posts.display: “Leave these men alone. Let them go! For if their purpose or endeavor is of human origin, it will fail. But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them. You may even find yourselves fighting against God.”
posts.caption: The apostles are arrested again, and the council wants them put to death. Then Gamaliel, one of the most respected Jewish teachers of the day, urges caution: a movement of merely human origin will fade on its own, but no one can fight God. Many readers see the rest of Acts as the outcome of his test, as the movement keeps spreading. Acts later says Paul had studied under him, and the Mishnah remembers him with great honor.

As the community grows, seven men are chosen to oversee the daily food distribution, which many churches see as the origin of deacons. One of them, Stephen, is accused of speaking against the temple and the law of Moses and brought before the Sanhedrin. As false witnesses testify, the council sees that his face is "like the face of an angel." Many commentators read it as a sign that God is with him; some recall Moses, whose face shone after meeting God.

Stephen's long speech before the council ends with him dragged out of the city and stoned, the first Christian martyr, from the Greek martys, "witness." He dies the way Jesus dies in Luke's Gospel: entrusting his spirit to the Lord and praying that his killers be forgiven. "Fell asleep" was an early Christian way of describing death, voicing hope of resurrection. Those stoning him lay their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.

Persecution scatters the believers, and Philip, one of the Seven, ends up on a desert road toward Gaza. There he meets a royal treasurer from Ethiopia, probably meaning the kingdom of Kush in today's Sudan, reading Isaiah aloud in his chariot. His honest answer turns the scene: he wants to understand, but needs a guide. Starting from that passage, about a servant led like a sheep to the slaughter, Philip tells him about Jesus, and the man is baptized by the roadside.

Saul, the young man who watched Stephen die, is on the road to Damascus with authority to arrest followers of "the Way," an early name for the movement. A light from heaven flashes around him, and the persecutor meets the one he is persecuting. The question carries the point: Jesus says Saul is persecuting him, not just his followers, and Christians read this as Jesus standing with his people. Saul, better known as Paul, will become the central figure of Acts.

posts.display: At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and his sight was restored. He got up and was baptized.
posts.caption: Saul arrives in Damascus blind and goes three days without eating or drinking. A believer named Ananias is told in a vision to go to him and objects, knowing Saul's reputation, but goes anyway and greets him as "Brother Saul." As Saul's sight returns, he is baptized into the very movement he came to crush, and many readers see his blindness and healing as a picture of his inner change. This verse gave English the phrase about scales falling from someone's eyes.

Peter is praying on a rooftop in Joppa, today's Jaffa, when he sees a sheet lowered from heaven full of animals, including ones Jewish food laws called unclean, and is told to eat. He refuses, and the voice answers with this, three times over. At that moment, messengers arrive from a Roman officer named Cornelius. Peter comes to see that the vision is about people as well as food: God is opening the door to non-Jews.

Cornelius is a Roman centurion who worships Israel's God but is not Jewish, and Jewish custom would have kept Peter from visiting a non-Jew's home. Peter goes anyway, and his sermon opens with what he has learned: God's welcome is not limited to one people. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit comes on Cornelius's household. In Acts, this is when the message decisively reaches the Gentiles, meaning non-Jews.

posts.display: The disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.
posts.caption: Believers scattered by persecution reach Antioch, one of the great cities of the Roman Empire (today Antakya, in southern Turkey), and start sharing the message with Greeks too. Barnabas brings Saul from Tarsus, and they teach there for a year. This is where the name Christians still use began, in a church of Jews and non-Jews together. Many scholars think "Christian," meaning something like "Christ's people," started as a nickname used by outsiders.

King Herod Agrippa I, a grandson of Herod the Great, has executed the apostle James and jailed Peter, chained between two soldiers on the night before his trial. Meanwhile the church is praying earnestly for him. Luke tells the rescue as God's answer to those prayers: an angel, a light, falling chains. Peter goes to the house where they are praying, and the servant girl Rhoda is so overjoyed at his voice that she forgets to open the gate.

The church in Antioch is worshiping and fasting when, Luke says, the Holy Spirit calls Barnabas and Saul to a new work. Luke presents the mission as the Spirit's initiative, given to a church at prayer. It begins what is often called Paul's first missionary journey, to Cyprus and then into today's Turkey. Saul was his Hebrew name and Paul (Paulus) his Roman one; from here on, the narrator calls him Paul.

In Lystra, in today's central Turkey, Paul heals a man who had never walked, and the crowd decides Barnabas and Paul are the gods Zeus and Hermes in human form. The priest of Zeus even brings bulls to sacrifice. The two insist they are only human. Speaking to people who didn't know the Jewish scriptures, they point to rain and harvests as signs of God's goodness.

posts.display: “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they said.
posts.caption: Soon after the crowd in Lystra tries to worship Paul and Barnabas, opponents win it over: Paul is stoned, dragged out of the city and left for dead. Yet he gets up, and the two retrace their route through the new churches. Their message to the believers is honest: following Jesus will not spare them hardship, and Paul still bears the bruises. They also appoint elders, in Greek presbyteroi, the root of "presbyter" and "priest."

Must non-Jewish believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses? Jesus' first followers were all Jews, so to many it seemed essential. Leaders meet in Jerusalem, usually dated around AD 49, and James, whom Paul calls "the Lord's brother," gives this judgment: Gentiles can belong without first becoming Jewish. They are asked only to avoid a few things, such as food offered to idols and eating blood. Many historians see this as a turning point in the movement's spread among non-Jews.

Paul, now traveling with Silas and young Timothy, keeps finding his plans blocked, until at Troas, on the coast of today's Turkey, he has this vision. Luke presents it as God's direction: the closed doors were steering him somewhere new. Macedonia is in northern Greece, so this is Paul's first step into Europe. In the next verse the narrator switches from "they" to "we," and tradition reads these "we" passages as the author joining the journey.

In Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia, Paul finds women gathered to pray by the river on the Sabbath. Lydia, from Thyatira in today's Turkey, deals in purple cloth, a costly luxury, and is a "worshiper of God," a non-Jew drawn to Israel's God. Luke credits her response to God, who "opened her heart." She is often called the first recorded convert in Europe, and her home becomes the new church's base.

Paul frees a slave girl from a spirit used for fortune-telling, and her owners, angry at losing their income, have Paul and Silas beaten and locked in the stocks. At midnight, instead of despairing, they are singing, and the other prisoners are listening. Christians have long drawn on this scene as a picture of joy in suffering. An earthquake throws open the doors, and the jailer, about to take his own life, asks how to be saved and is baptized that night.

Driven out of Thessalonica and Berea, Paul reaches Athens, the old center of Greek philosophy, and is invited to explain himself at the Areopagus, a hill near the Acropolis and the council named after it. Instead of attacking the city's religion, he starts from something he saw on his walk: an altar to an unknown god. His point is that the God they sense but cannot name is the one he has come to proclaim.

Paul's speech in Athens quotes Greek poets, not the Hebrew scriptures. His point is that God is not far off or made by human hands: all people live within God's reach and owe their life to God, something the Greeks' own poets glimpsed. "We are His offspring" comes from Aratus, a poet from Paul's home region of Cilicia; the first line is often attributed to Epimenides. When Paul mentions resurrection, some scoff, but a few believe.

In Corinth, a busy Greek trading city, Paul makes tents with Priscilla and Aquila, a Jewish couple expelled from Rome by Emperor Claudius. Facing fierce opposition, he receives this vision: keep speaking, you are not alone, and many here will listen. Encouraged, he stays a year and a half. An inscription found at Delphi dates the governor Gallio, mentioned a few verses later, to around AD 51, one of the firmest dates in Paul's life.

Paul spends more than two years in Ephesus, on Turkey's west coast, a city famous for magic, where written spells were even called "Ephesian letters." Here new believers who had practiced magic burn their scrolls in public. The point is the cost: a drachma was a silver coin worth about a day's wage, so this was a fortune given up to make a clean break. Paul's success also hurt the trade in shrines of the goddess Artemis and set off a riot.

On his way to Jerusalem, Paul stops at the port of Miletus and sends for the church leaders from Ephesus to say goodbye. He tells them that prison and hardship await him, and that his own safety matters less than finishing the work Jesus gave him. "Finish my course" is a runner's image of completing a race, one Paul also uses in his letters. Of his major speeches in Acts, this is the only one given to fellow believers.

Paul ends his farewell to the Ephesian leaders by reminding them that he worked with his own hands to support himself and others. His point is that leaders should give rather than take, and look after the weak. He backs it with a saying of Jesus that appears in none of the four Gospels, one of the few recorded outside them. Afterward they all kneel to pray, weep, and walk him to his ship.

At Caesarea, a prophet named Agabus ties his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to show that Paul will be bound in Jerusalem. Paul's friends, the narrator among them, beg him not to go. His reply shows he has counted the cost: he will go anyway, ready even to die. Many readers see a parallel with Jesus in Luke's Gospel, who also set out for Jerusalem knowing what awaited him.

A crowd attacks Paul in the temple courts, and Roman soldiers take him into custody. About to be flogged for questioning, he raises his citizenship, and everything stops, since Roman law protected citizens from such treatment. The commander says he paid a high price for his own citizenship; Paul was born a citizen. His name, Claudius Lysias, suggests he bought it under Emperor Claudius.

Brought before the Sanhedrin, Paul splits the council by raising the resurrection, which Pharisees believed in and Sadducees rejected. That night, back in the Roman barracks, he has this vision. At a low point, the promise is that his work is not over: he will bear witness in Rome, and the rest of Acts follows that promise. Soon more than forty men swear to kill him, and Paul is moved to Caesarea under heavy guard.

In Caesarea, a Roman port on the coast of today's Israel, Paul is held for trial before the governor Felix. Felix and his wife Drusilla, a Jewish princess, listen to Paul privately, until he turns to righteousness, self-control and judgment. The scene turns the tables: the prisoner speaks freely, and the powerful judge is the one afraid, putting off the hard questions for later. Felix hoped for a bribe and left Paul in prison for two years.

Two years on, a new governor, Festus, proposes moving Paul's trial to Jerusalem, though his accusers had plotted to ambush him on the way. Paul says he isn't dodging justice, but he won't be handed over unfairly, so he uses his right as a Roman citizen to appeal to the emperor himself. That appeal is how Paul finally gets to Rome. The "Caesar" at the time was Nero. Festus replies, "To Caesar you will go!"

Before he leaves for Rome, Paul speaks before King Herod Agrippa II, a great-grandson of Herod the Great, and tells his conversion story, the third account of it in Acts. The king brushes him off, and Paul's answer shows his heart: he wishes everyone listening could share his faith, though not his chains. The King James Version famously renders the king's reply, "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian."

Paul sails for Rome as a prisoner, late in the season: Luke notes it was already "after the Fast," meaning Yom Kippur in the autumn, when sailing grew dangerous. A violent northeaster drives the ship off course for days without sun or stars, and all hope is given up. Then the prisoner becomes the one giving courage: an angel, Paul says, has promised that everyone on board will survive, and he trusts God to keep that promise.

After two weeks adrift, the ship runs aground and breaks apart, but all 276 people on board reach shore alive. The island is Malta. The narrator, who was on board, remembers the welcome: strangers with no reason to help soaked sailors and prisoners show them "extraordinary kindness." When a viper fastens onto Paul's hand at the fire and he is unharmed, the islanders decide he must be a god. Malta still honors Paul.

After three months on Malta, Paul sails on to Italy, and believers from Rome come out along the Appian Way to meet him. His arrival fulfills both the promise that he would testify in Rome and the outline set out at the start of Acts: from Jerusalem to the heart of the empire. Yet he comes not as a free traveler but as a prisoner under guard. Paul had written his letter to the Romans a few years earlier.

Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome, still welcoming visitors and teaching. The very last word in Greek is akolytos, "unhindered": Paul is in chains, but the message is not. Acts never says what happened to him next; early Christian tradition holds he was executed in Rome under Nero. Many readers take the open ending as the point: the story carries on with the church. That's the book of Acts. Thank you for reading it with me.
